source_document.body:
S&P Global Ratings raised its long-term issuer credit rating on Canadian Pacific Kansas City Ltd. (NYSE: CP) to A- from BBB+. It also raised the rating on the railroad’s unsecured debt to A- from BBB+.
S&P on Tuesday said CPKC has kept delivering solid results despite economic and trade headwinds, and noted a stable outlook. It said this shows the strength of the company’s diversity and growth opportunities after its acquisition of Kansas City Southern in 2023. The upgrade follows S&P’s December 2025 move to a positive outlook on the BBB+ rating.
Growth ahead of competitors
Since 2022, CPKC’s pro forma volumes, revenue and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) have grown faster than those of the other North American Class 1 railroads, S&P said. It expects that to continue. The agency credited the KCS merger and subsequent integration, and service improvements. It also credited the only single-line rail network linking Canada, the United States and Mexico.
S&P expects volumes to rise by a low-single-digit percentage on truck-to-rail conversion on U.S.-Mexico lanes; intermodal partnerships with Maersk (OTC: AMKBY )-Hapag-Lloyd’s ( HLAG.DE ) Gemini cooperation, Schneider National (NYSE: SNDR ) and Americold (NYSE: COLD ); and coal volumes recovered from Elk Valley Resources, business CPKC lost to Canadian National (NYSE: CNI ) in 2021.
S&P said these gains should more than offset tougher Canadian grain comparisons, as well as competitive pressure from a potential Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP )–Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC ) merger.
Year to date through Nov. 21, revenue ton miles were up about 4.2%. Grain, minerals and consumer products offset flat or falling industrial volumes. About 41% of revenue comes from goods crossing the Canada-U.S. or Mexico-U.S. border. Even so, S&P expects tariffs to cut revenue by less than 1% this year. Tariff-exposed lanes make up under 20% of freight revenue.
Financial forecasts
S&P expects the following indicators to develop over the next few years:
Adjusted funds from operations (FFO) to debt of 23%–25%
Adjusted debt to EBITDA of 2.8x–3.0x
Mid-single-digit annual EBITDA growth
Capital spending of 16%–17% of revenue
Annual free operating cash flow of C$3.5–C$4 billion ($2.46-2.81 billion), or 12%–15% of debt
Net leverage was 3.2x at Sept. 30, 2026. S&P expects it to reach management’s 2.75x target by the end of next year. It also expects CPKC to spend at least $1.76 billion a year on buybacks and raise dividends about 10% a year, adjusting buybacks to stay near the leverage target.
What could change the rating
S&P warned it could downgrade CPKC within 24 months if FFO to debt falls below 23% or free operating cash flow to debt falls below 10% on a sustained basis. That could follow a more aggressive financial policy or weaker operations. An upgrade would need sustained FFO to debt above 35% and free operating cash flow to debt above 18%, along with more conservative financial policies.
CP shares closed Nov. 24 at $92.82, up 2.42%. Its market capitalization is about $80.7 billion. The stock has traded between $70.01 and $96.90 over the past 52 weeks.
Analyst sentiment on the company is bullish. Of eight ratings tracked, six are bullish and two neutral, with none bearish. The average price target is about $111.38, and the median is $103. Targets range from $93 to $145.
Why It Matters: A higher credit rating usually lowers borrowing costs and widens the pool of investors who can hold a company’s debt. It signals that a rating agency sees the post-merger railroad as financially stronger and more resilient, even with trade uncertainty.
